One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade”, Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture, and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX. In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. (Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) page.text_excerpt: Daemonic Dispatches Musings from Colin Percival The Duty of a Scholar On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state. There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly. This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. page.description: When your database CPU is at 100%, what is it actually doing? Memory stalls, CPU caches, and how radix partitioning makes GROUP BY faster.

We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%? The answer is usually memory. Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. This article will land much better with a concrete example, but I am drawing a blank here, so you gotta just blindly trust my say so! When implementing a software module, it’s often a case that you are writing a public function foo, and at least part of what foo does is already handled by another public function bar. The DRY instinct encourages you to call bar() from within foo. This usually creates problems down the line. Instead, create a new private function and refactor both foo and bar to call that shared helper: // BAD pub fn foo() void { return bar(.{ .frobnicate = true }); } pub fn bar(options: struct { frobnicate: bool = false, }) void { // ... } // GOOD pub fn foo() void { return helper(.frobnicate); } pub fn bar() void { return helper(.transmogrify); } fn helper(mode: enum { frobnicate, transmogrify }) void { // ... } Rationale: the goal of a public API is to provide an interface that works best at the call site. If parts of public API are re-used to implement the rest of the API, then there’s a tension between making the interface convenient for the outside user and making it convenient to use from within abstraction itself. Namely, functions tend to grow optional parameters that should never be set by the user. Crucially, the parameter growth and interface degradation can happen after the original code sharing. By proactively making the shared implementation private, the tension is defused. You still might need to tinker with helper signature until it does everything it needs to do, but, because the helper is private, this is a cheap, local change. A notable exception to this rule of thumb are “shortcut” APIs, where a public function is defined as a commonly used chain of calls to other public functions. page.text_excerpt: #1 Trusted Cybersecurity News Platform Followed by 5.80+ million    Get Updates Home Threat Intelligence Vulnerabilities Cyber Attacks Webinars Expert Insights Awards   Linux Kernel TCP Flaw With 9.8 CVSS Score Affects Ubuntu, Red Hat and Other Distributions Swati KhandelwalOct 29, 2026 Vulnerability / Linux A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and other Linux distributions. The kernel's own CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Anthropic said on October 27 that its AI model wrote an exploit that uses the flaw to let a remote attacker with no credentials run commands as root on Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. As of October 29, Ubuntu and RHEL have not released a fixed kernel. Red Hat, Amazon, Oracle, and SUSE score the flaw between 5.9 and 8.1, lower than the kernel team's 9.8. The flaw is a race condition in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections. It can make the kernel read memory it has already freed, a bug type known as a use-after-free. The kernel fix credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge with reporting the bug. Neither the CVE record nor the fix mentions multipath TCP (MPTCP). The link between that feature and this bug comes from Anthropic's post. MPTCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. On Linux, an application must request MPTCP when it opens a socket. As of Go 1.24, Go programs do so by default for the sockets they listen on, the Go Security Team said on October 29. Anthropic's post says the flaw "was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches." For distribution users, that fix arrives only in the vendor's kernel package. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux have shipped fixed packages, at least for some of their kernels, but Ubuntu and RHEL have not. page.description: How simple circuits can create complex behaviors
page.text_excerpt: MYRIAD Let’s Build a Brain By Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article. All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors? This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle. In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors. Light eaters Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light. The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses. It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper. By wiring the first sensory neuron to the second motor neuron, we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit: The anatomy of a spark With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light. Can it find the light? If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss. Over time, their paths look like this: Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better… Adding an eye Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn. What if we give it another eye and flipper? With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this: Hmm… that didn’t work. Defenders of polyamory emphasize that it always requires consent from every participant. It’s different from adultery, they say, because everyone knows what’s happening and nobody objects.
